w: A small national park perched right at Burleigh Heads, wedged between the Gold Coast's high-rises and the surf - proof the coastline still keeps a wild headland or two, even this close to the strip.
s: A wild headland squeezed between high-rises and surf.
_facts: A small national park at Burleigh Heads in the City of Gold Coast, South East Queensland

w: Its name means 'Conspicuous Mountain' in the local Aboriginal language - quietly funny, since Mount Nimmel is dwarfed by its Springbrook hinterland neighbours, Tamborine Mountain and Mount Cougal's twin peaks. Protected within Springbrook National Park, all the same.
s: A mountain named 'Conspicuous' that really isn't.
_facts: A small mountain in Springbrook, part of the Gold Coast hinterland
Its indigenous name means 'Conspicuous Mountain', considered ironic given how small it is next to Springbrook Mountain, Tamborine Mountain and Mount Cougal's twin peaks

w: Wedged between the Nerang River and a golf course at Benowa, these gardens started life as plain old Rosser Park before growing into a proper botanic collection - raised vegetable beds and herb gardens included, teaching Gold Coast kids how food actually gets grown.
s: From plain old Rosser Park to a proper botanic garden.
_facts: Formerly known as Rosser Park Regional Botanic Gardens, and before that simply Rosser Park, on Ashmore Road, Benowa
Bounded by the Nerang River to the south-west and the Royal Pines Resort Golf Course to the north
Includes raised vegetable, fruit and herb gardens alongside a large variety of plants

w: Alex Griffiths opened this sanctuary in 1947 purely to stop wild lorikeets eating his flower crops - he fed them instead, and they kept coming by the flock. Heritage-listed since 2009, it's grown a wildlife hospital and a 1964 miniature railway, but the lorikeet feed still draws the crowds.
s: Started in 1947 just to stop lorikeets eating flowers.
_facts: Heritage-listed zoological garden at 28 Tomewin Street, Currumbin, built from 1947 onwards
Added to the Queensland Heritage Register on 18 September 2009
Opened in 1947 by Alex Griffiths as the Currumbin Bird Sanctuary, originally to stop lorikeets damaging his flower crops
Known for daily feeding of large flocks of free-flying wild rainbow lorikeets
Now includes a miniature railway operating since 1964, a wildlife hospital, and the Lost Valley precinct opened in 2017
